i have an idea for something called. crawl_early_end or crawl_window_end. the vision behind something like crawl_early_end is to return it optionally alongside data and next token in crawlers. if we have a crawl that needs to get 45 days, but the filter only supports 30 days (or for some other reason we only want to get a smaller window of data), we can just use the 30 days in the filter and return data, next token, and crawl_early_end = start + 30 days

we do have to do this already sometimes, but the solution to that is just make the page token more complex which sucks (and is annoying to deal with for in progress crawls). i find myself having to do this a lot when doing maintenance stuff for stale schedules and it'd be nice to do a more permanent solve than manual hand holding. finale get orders is an example

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- integration-api-validator: Validates an external integration's API before any code is written. Characterizes transport, auth, pagination, response format, token refresh, and webhook style; identifies the closest existing integration as exemplar via parallel Explore searches. Use when starting a new integration via /plan-integration, or ad-hoc to re-characterize an existing integration whose source API has changed (vendor migration, new endpoints, deprecation). Outputs `.claude/references/{name}/api-summary.md`. (Tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, Grep, Glob)

- integration-data-seeder: Seeds a vendor's writes-safe sandbox with enough test data for downstream function-writer validation — products, inventory, orders distributed across states, returns, inbound shipments — and attempts state transitions (ship, cancel, process). Records under api-summary.md "Sandbox seeding" what was created and any state transitions that couldn't be driven via API (vendor UI required, real carrier needed, etc.). Spawned by the orchestrator after `integration-api-validator` finishes characterization, when the validator's reads turned up a thin or empty sandbox. Single-pass agent — runs once per integration build. (Tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, Grep, Glob)

- integration-function-writer: Implements one coherent unit of integration code — either a single data function (get_orders, get_inventory, write_order, etc.) or the auth bundle (get_integration_secret + <name>_request + validate_integration_secret). Iterates with yarn crawl + yarn test until validated. Standard path is via /plan-integration after the api-validator has produced api-summary.md. Can also be invoked ad-hoc for a single-method add to an existing integration when the exemplar is already known. Adheres strictly to .claude/references/integration-patterns.md. (Tools: Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- integration-reviewer: Reviews a single unit of integration code (one data function, the auth bundle, or a single test file) against `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md`. Pattern-matches against the exemplar from api-summary.md when present. Runs targeted `yarn test`. Emits a structured BLOCK / APPROVE / APPROVE_WITH_NOTES verdict. Has no edit access — surfaces findings only. Use after each integration-function-writer invocation in /plan-integration, OR ad-hoc to review a single file or diff when debugging an integration, investigating a customer issue, or pre-PR. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

Unrelated bugs found along the way become Linear cards, not PRs. Fully unattended, internal-only. Use when handed a Pylon issue id (UUID) in a routine session.

Two modes — compose a card from a freeform human ask (pick the Type label + integration/customer label, write a short human body), or file a caller-supplied spec verbatim (used by automated skills like stale-schedule-investigate, which own their own title grammar and labels). Always reads the live workspace label set and never invents labels. Use when asked to file/create/open a Linear issue, ticket, or card, and whenever another skill needs to create one. import base64
import copy
import json
import urllib
from collections import defaultdict
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from datetime import timedelta
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime

from config import (
    FINALE_CHANNEL_AS_WH_CUSTOMER_CONNECTIONS,
    FINALE_ORDER_FILTER_SECONDS,
)
from integrations.wms.WMSIntegration import WMSIntegration
from resources import InboundShipment, Order, Product
from resources.wms.inventory import InventoryItem

)

)

    def support(self):
        return "service@finaleinventory.com"

    def get_integration_secret(self, body):
        return {
            "access_token": f"{body['api_key']}:{body['api_secret']}",
            "account_name": body["account_name"],
        }

    def me(self):
        return {
            "username": self.integration_secret["access_token"].split(":")[0],
            "account_name": self.integration_secret["account_name"],
        }

    def safe_me(self):
        return self.me()

    def safe_integration_secret_keys(self):
        return ["account_name"]

    def validate_integration_secret(self):
        return self.finale_request("facility")

    def validate_financial_info(self):
        return False

    def validate_financial_info_with_line_items(self):
        return False

    def base_url(self):
        return (
            f"https://app.finaleinventory.com/{self.integration_secret['account_name']}"
        )

    def finale_request(
        self, path, method="GET", is_list=True, is_report=False, **kwargs
    ):
        access_token = base64.b64encode(
            self.integration_secret["access_token"].encode("utf-8")
        ).decode("utf-8")

        headers = {
            "Authorization": f"Basic {access_token}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        }
        if is_report:
            url = f"{self.base_url()}/doc/{path}"
        else:
            url_encoded_path = urllib.parse.quote(path)
            url = f"{self.base_url()}/api/{url_encoded_path}"
        session = get_request_session()

        @retry(3, "Finale")
        def retry_method():
            response = session.request(method, url, headers=headers, **kwargs)
            if response.status_code == 429:
                # finale rate-limits bursts of requests (order enrichment fans out many
                # concurrent shipment fetches), so retry rather than aborting the crawl
                retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                if not retry_after:
                    wait_seconds = 10
                elif retry_after.isdigit():
                    wait_seconds = int(retry_after)
                else:
                    # retry-after may be an http-date instead of seconds; use the delay it
                    # implies, falling back to a short pause if it won't parse
                    try:
                        retry_dt = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                        wait_seconds = max(0, int((retry_dt - now()).total_seconds()))
                    except (TypeError, ValueError):
                        wait_seconds = 10

The primitive already exists — it's called `latest_data_override`, and it does exactly what you're describing.

`celery_tasks/crawler.py:431-436`: on the last page (no `next_token`, no `pending_page_token`), the watermark written to `latest_data` is `rsp.get("latest_data_override", end_time_str)`. It's declared in `crawl_schema` at `resources/base_resource.py:524`, and two integrations use it:

- `integrations/wms/fba/integration.py:748-761` — inventory ledger: if `query_end < end`, it either overrides the watermark (last short window) or falls back to a page token.
- `integrations/carrier/royal-mail/integration.py:312` — sets it to `page_token["original_end_time"]`.

So Finale get_orders could drop its page-token chaining (`integration.py:528-577`) and instead return `{"data": ..., "next_token": None, "latest_data_override": filter_end}`. The scheduler picks `latest_data` up as the next `start_time_str` (`lambda_handlers/scheduler.py:104-109`), and `current_crawl_start/end` get cleared since `next_token` is None.

Two things stop this from being the permanent solve you want, and both are worth fixing at the framework level:

**1. The guards are hand-rolled per integration.** FBA has to write `and not sync_job_id` itself, because the sync-job branch (`crawler.py:415-425`) never reads `latest_data_override` — a sync job owes an explicit range and has no watermark to advance, so an early end there silently drops data. If the framework raised on `latest_data_override` during a sync job (or auto-converted it to a `next_token`), integrations wouldn't each need to remember. Same for the "override must be within `[start, end]` and strictly greater than `start`" check — FBA writes that inline as `start < query_end < requested_end`.

**2. Backlog drains at window-per-crawl instead of everything-in-one-task.** This is the real behavior change and the reason it isn't a free swap. Page-token chaining drains an arbitrary backlog inside one celery task; early-end advances exactly one window per scheduler tick. Finale's default 4h window against orders' 1h crawl frequency catches up at 4x wall clock, which is fine, but a connection with `FINALE_ORDER_FILTER_SECONDS` tuned down (`config.py`) could fall below 1x and never converge — and `latest_data` is what `stale_schedule_marker.py:446-464` keys staleness off, so it'd go stale and stay stale. A framework version should log the implied drain rate, or better, keep paginating within the task and only early-end when the task is out of budget (heartbeat/visibility timeout), which gets you both properties.

Want me to write this up as a Linear card, or implement the framework-side piece (validation + sync-job handling + drain-rate warning) and convert Finale as the first caller?

content.text:
Doable, and the loop change is the easy half. Here's the shape and the three things that actually bite.

**The loop.** In `crawler.py:341`, a window commit is just a token reset plus an advanced start:

```python
while next_token:
    ...
    data, next_token = rsp["data"], rsp["next_token"]
    window_end = rsp.get("crawl_window_end")
    ...  # existing update_crawl_items, with set_latest_data = window_end
    if window_end:
        commit_watermark_barrier(connection_id, function_name, window_end)
        start_time_dt = str_to_dt(window_end)
        next_token = "default"
```

`first_loop` stays False, so Finale's party-group/facility/kit setup doesn't rerun per window. Enforce the invariant in `validate_crawl` (`resources/base_resource.py:615`) — `crawl_window_end` and `next_token` are mutually exclusive — plus a `window_end > current window start` check, which is your infinite-loop guard.

I'd keep this as a new key rather than overloading `latest_data_override`. The existing one means "stop here", which is genuinely what FBA's last short window and royal-mail's async report need; yours means "commit here and ask me again".

**Draining is the real work.** `submit.tasks_started`/`tasks_finished` is one flat pair per (connection, function), so pipelining window 2's pages into it while window 1's watermark is armed makes `tasks_started == tasks_finished` (`utils/boto.py:2772`) mean nothing. Simplest correct answer is a barrier: arm `set_latest_data = window_end`, then poll the scheduler row until `latest_data == window_end` before starting the next window. The barrier has to also do the tail's own check itself — if the last submitter finished before you armed `set_latest_data`, nobody re-evaluates and you'd hang — so factor `crawler.py:535-548` into a helper both the barrier and the tail call. Bound the wait and raise on timeout; that's safe precisely because the last committed watermark is durable. The heartbeat thread is already running, so the schedule won't go stale while you sit there.

The alternative (no barrier) is a `window_end → tracking_ids` map on the crawl item, committing the earliest window when its set empties. More throughput, meaningfully more bookkeeping. I'd ship the barrier first — windows are coarse, and the latency is one lambda round-trip per window.

**Two things that will silently break if you don't touch them.**

`finished_last_page` in `lambda_handlers/submitter.py:201` currently means "crawl is over", and it gates the historical-sync webhook and the force-sync-completed webhook. With per-window commits it fires on window 1 of a first crawl. Arm a `submit.is_final_commit` bool alongside `set_latest_data` and AND it in.

And `store_current_crawl_params`: the scheduler prefers `current_crawl_start` over `latest_data` (`lambda_handlers/scheduler.py:107-112`), so on a resume it would re-run from window 1's start. Write `current_crawl_start = window_end` at each commit, leave `current_crawl_end` pinned to the original end, clear both on final exit. That gets you the property you're actually after: a task that dies at window 5 of 270 resumes at window 5, with no page token to go stale.

**Bug you already have.** `crawler.py:541` writes `"latest_data": end_time_str`, but the submitter writes `crawl_item["submit"]["set_latest_data"]` (`submitter.py:206`). So when the crawler wins the race, today's `latest_data_override` is discarded and the watermark jumps to the full `end` — FBA's ledger skips whatever was in `[query_end, end]`. Needs fixing regardless, and the windowing design depends on it.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/harshanandiwada/workspace/early-crawl-end/.claude/skills/create-linear-issue

# Create Linear issue

The single place that creates a Linear issue. Every flow that files a card routes through here, so the team defaults, label validation, and the `save_issue` call live in one spot. Call it directly from a person's freeform ask, or from another skill that has already composed the card it wants.

Defaults: team **Trackstar hq**, team default status (omit `state`), no assignee unless one is given.

**In scope:** create a new card. **Out of scope:** editing or closing existing issues (that path passes an `id` to `save_issue` directly and isn't this skill).

## Two modes

- **Compose** — a person hands you a freeform ask. You pick the labels and write the body. This is the default; the [Compose](#compose-mode) section below covers it.
- **Spec** — another skill hands you a card it already composed. The caller owns the title, body, and labels; you validate the labels against the live set and file it as given, without rewriting. See [Spec mode](#spec-mode).

Both modes read the live label set and never invent a label. Both end at the same `save_issue` call.

---

## Compose mode

### Input

A free-text ask, plus optional hints the caller may pass inline:

- `priority` — none | low | medium | high | urgent
- `assignee` — a name, email, or "me"
- `labels` — extra labels to force on (each must still exist in the workspace)
- `project` — project name or slug

If the ask is one vague line and you genuinely can't tell what the work is, ask one clarifying question before filing. Otherwise proceed.

### 1. Read the live label set

Pull the current set and match against it:

```
mcp__Linear__list_issue_labels  (team: "Trackstar hq", limit: 250)
```

If the response reports more labels than it returned (`hasNextPage` true), page through with the returned cursor until you've read the whole set — validating against a partial set drops a valid label in compose mode and hard-stops a real-but-unread label in spec mode. Labels are added often (every new integration adds one), so read them at run time rather than trusting any list baked into this file. Never invent a label.

### 2. Pick the labels that matter

Two kinds of label carry the weight. Get these right; everything else is optional.

**a. Exactly one Type label.** The **Type** group is the parent grouping every card needs one of. Match the ask to the label whose description fits:

| Type label | Use when the ask is… |
|---|---|
| Integration Maintenance | work on an existing integration — bug fix, data issue, a new flow or field |
| Integration Request | a brand-new WMS / cart / channel integration ask |
| Product / API | new product or API capability, SDK, MCP |
| Platform | infra, reliability, ops, dependencies, internal tooling |
| Frontend | eevee / pokecenter / website work |
| Docs | documentation work |

These descriptions live on the labels themselves — if the live set has changed, trust the label's own description over this table.

**b. The customer or integration-name label, if one exists for it.** When the card is about a specific integration (Katana, Cin7, Flexport, …) or a specific customer, add that name label — but only if that exact label is already in the workspace. If the integration or customer has no label yet, skip it rather than creating one.

### 3. Optional extra tags

Only if they clearly apply, and only from the live set: **quality of life**, **Improvement**, **Feature**, **Bug** (confirmed) or **Bug (potential)** (unconfirmed), **deprecation**, **scheduling logic**. The Type label plus the customer / integration name is usually the whole story.

Honor any `labels` hint the caller passed, but: drop any that don't exist in the live set; drop any automation-only label even when it's named explicitly (see next line); and keep the card to exactly one Type label total. If the hint names a Type-group label, it replaces the one you picked rather than stacking on top — never attach two Type labels. If the hint names two different Type labels, ask which one. Say which you dropped or replaced, and why.

**Don't** apply the automation-only labels in compose mode — `stale-schedule`, `class:*`, `function-*`, `agent-investigation` — neither from your own pick nor from a `labels` hint. Those belong to the automated flows, which come in through spec mode with the labels already set. A human-filed card carrying `stale-schedule` would enter the stale-schedule reconciliation queue and can suppress a real investigation or trigger a spurious auto-close on the matched schedules.

### 4. Write the body — short and human

Follow `.claude/rules/communications.md`. Lead with the point in one sentence (what and why), then the minimum supporting detail a teammate needs to pick it up.

- No em-dashes. No AI filler ("seamless", "robust", "in order to", "Let me know…").
- One-read test: a teammate who didn't write it gets it in one pass.
- Don't pad with empty headers (Background / Acceptance Criteria) unless the ask genuinely has them. A two-sentence card is fine.
- If the ask lists concrete requirements, keep them as a short bullet list. Don't invent scope.

Title: a plain, specific summary in sentence case, no trailing punctuation, no ticket-id prefix.

### 5. Map the hints

- **priority** → none=0, low=4, medium=3, high=2, urgent=1. Omit if not given.
- **assignee** → pass through as given; omit entirely if none (no default assignee).
- **project** → pass the name or slug if given.
- **status** → omit `state` so the team default applies.

### 6. Confirm, then create

Show the drafted card — title, body, labels, priority, assignee, project — in the chat and ask the caller to confirm, unless they already said to just file it. Then go to [Create](#create-the-save_issue-call).

---

## Spec mode

A skill that needs a card composes it, then hands the spec here. The caller's format is authoritative — its title grammar, body (including any machine-readable block), and label choices pass through unchanged.

Every card still carries exactly one Type label, the same standard as compose mode — the only difference is the caller picked it, so this skill validates and files rather than choosing. The caller's labels include that Type label plus whatever else it needs (for example, stale-schedule cards use `Integration Maintenance` + `stale-schedule` + one `class:*`).

The caller passes: `title`, `description` (markdown, already composed), `labels` (names), and optionally `state`, `assignee`, `project`, `priority`.

1. **Read the live label set** (same call as compose step 1).
2. **Validate every label in the spec exists, and hard-stop if one doesn't.** Automation labels (`stale-schedule`, `class:*`, `agent-investigation`, …) are expected here and pass through once confirmed present. If any spec label is missing from the live set, don't invent it, don't drop it, and don't call `save_issue` — stop and report the missing label to the caller so it creates the label or corrects the spec, then retry. These labels are load-bearing: a stale-schedule card that lands without its `stale-schedule` + `class:*` labels won't queue or reconcile, so filing it unclassified is worse than not filing.
3. **Check Type cardinality — exactly one Type-group label.** The standard holds in spec mode too. If the spec carries no Type label or more than one, hard-stop the same way (don't file) and report it to the caller to fix, then retry.
4. **Don't rewrite anything.** No editing the title or body, no adding or dropping labels, no imposing the human-body conventions. File it as given.
5. Go to [Create](#create-the-save_issue-call), then **return the new issue id and URL to the caller** so it can thread them into a PR, a pointer write, or a downstream comment.

No human confirmation step in spec mode — the calling skill already decided to file.

---

## Create (the `save_issue` call)

This is the only step in either mode that writes:

```
mcp__Linear__save_issue
  team: "Trackstar hq"
  title: <title>
  description: <body>
  labels: [<Type label / spec labels>, <name label if any>, <extras>]
  priority: <0-4, if given>
  assignee: <if given>
  project: <if given>
  state: <only if the caller gave one; otherwise omit for the team default>
```

Every card files to **Trackstar hq**, which is also the team the label set in step 1 is read from, so validation and the write always look at the same labels.

Don't pass `id` — that updates an existing issue, which is out of scope. Report back the new issue identifier and URL from the result.

---

## Example (compose)

Ask: `file a card: Katana get_inventory is dropping the committed quantity on bundles`

- Type label: **Integration Maintenance** (work on an existing integration)
- Name label: **Katana** (exists in the set)
- Title: `Katana get_inventory drops committed quantity on bundles`
- Body:
  > Katana's `get_inventory` is reporting committed quantity as 0 for bundle SKUs, even when the bundle has open orders. Single SKUs look right. Likely the bundle branch isn't reading the committed field. Needs a crawl against a connection with bundle inventory to confirm the source value, then a fix in the mapping.

ARGUMENTS: crawler tail overwrites latest_data_override with end_time_str — when the crawler (not the submitter) observes the last submit task draining, celery_tasks/crawler.py:541 writes latest_data = end_time_str instead of crawl_item["submit"]["set_latest_data"], discarding the integration's latest_data_override. Affects FBA get_inventory_ledger (skips ledger entries between query_end and end) and royal-mail invoice line items. labels: bug, integration fba

input.title: Crawler tail overwrites latest_data_override with the full crawl end
input.description:
When a crawl finishes and the crawler (rather than the submitter) is the one that observes the last submit task draining, it writes `latest_data = end_time_str` instead of the watermark the integration asked for.

`celery_tasks/crawler.py:541` hardcodes `end_time_str`, while `lambda_handlers/submitter.py:206` correctly writes `crawl_item["submit"]["set_latest_data"]`. Both paths are reachable, so which watermark lands is a race: if every submitter lambda finishes before the crawler reaches its tail block, the integration's `latest_data_override` is discarded and the watermark jumps to the full crawl end.

Impact is silently skipped data in the gap between the override and the crawl end:

- FBA `get_inventory_ledger` (`integrations/wms/fba/integration.py:748-761`) sets the override to `query_end` when Amazon's last window comes up short. Losing it skips every ledger entry between `query_end` and `end`.
- Royal Mail invoice line items (`integrations/carrier/royal-mail/integration.py:312`) sets it to `page_token["original_end_time"]`.

Fix is to read `set_latest_data` off the crawl item in the tail block, same as the submitter does. Worth factoring the two commit paths into one helper so they can't drift again.

def test_windowed_crawl_advances_start_and_commits_each_window(
    store_crawl_params_connection_row,
    org_row,
    store_crawl_params_resource,
    now_mock,
    update_crawl_items_mock,
    mocker,
):
    # a window that ends early commits its own watermark and the crawl keeps going
    # from there, instead of the integration hiding the rest of the range in a token
    start_time_str = "2019-12-01T00:00:00Z"
    end_time_str = dt_to_str(now_mock.return_value)
    window_end = "2019-12-16T00:00:00Z"
    starts_seen = []

    def side_effect(
        resource,
        start,
        end,
        first_crawl,
        first_loop,
        page_token,
        local_submit,
        sync_job_id=None,
        notify_force_sync=False,
    ):
        starts_seen.append(start)
        if first_loop:
            page = {"next_token": None, "data": [], "crawl_window_end": window_end}
            return page, {}, {"submit_task_id_1"}
        return {"next_token": None, "data": []}, {}, {"submit_task_id_2"}

    mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.get_and_submit", side_effect=side_effect)
    wait_mock = mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.wait_for_window_commit")

    crawler.crawl_task(
        store_crawl_params_connection_row,
        org_row,
        "get_bills",
        False,
        start_time_str,
        end_time_str,
        None,
    )

    integration = store_crawl_params_resource.integration
    overlap = timedelta(minutes=integration.crawl_start_overlap_minutes)
    assert starts_seen == [
        str_to_dt(start_time_str) - overlap,
        str_to_dt(window_end),
    ]
    wait_mock.assert_called_once_with(
        store_crawl_params_connection_row["id"], "get_bills", window_end
    )

    window_calls = []
    final_calls = []
    for call_elem in update_crawl_items_mock.call_args_list:
        submit = call_elem[0][2].get("submit", {})
        if submit.get("set_latest_data") == window_end:
            window_calls.append(call_elem[0][2])
        elif submit.get("set_latest_data") == end_time_str:
            final_calls.append(call_elem[0][2])

    assert len(window_calls) == 1
    window_update = window_calls[0]
    assert window_update["submit"]["is_final_commit"] is False
    # the next crawl resumes at the window we committed, against the same end
    assert window_update["current_crawl_start"] == window_end
    assert window_update["current_crawl_end"] == end_time_str
    # the window is fully drained, so there is no in-window token to resume from
    assert window_update["latest_page_token"] is None

    assert len(final_calls) == 1
    assert final_calls[0]["submit"]["is_final_commit"] is True
    assert final_calls[0]["current_crawl_start"] is None


def test_windowed_crawl_rejects_window_end_past_the_crawl_end(
    store_crawl_params_connection_row,
    org_row,
    now_mock,
    mocker,
):
    # a window that claims more than the crawl asked for would skip data
    def side_effect(
        resource,
        start,
        end,
        first_crawl,
        first_loop,
        page_token,
        local_submit,
        sync_job_id=None,
        notify_force_sync=False,
    ):
        page = {
            "next_token": None,
            "data": [],
            "crawl_window_end": "2020-06-01T00:00:00Z",
        }
        return page, {}, {"submit_task_id_1"}

    mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.get_and_submit", side_effect=side_effect)

    with pytest.raises(PokedexException, match="not inside the remaining crawl range"):
        crawler.crawl_task(
            store_crawl_params_connection_row,
            org_row,
            "get_bills",
            False,
            "2019-12-01T00:00:00Z",
            dt_to_str(now_mock.return_value),
            None,
        )


def test_wait_for_window_commit_writes_the_watermark_the_submitter_missed(mocker):
    # the last submitter can finish before the watermark is armed, so the crawler
    # has to be able to write it itself or the window would never commit
    window_end = "2019-12-16T00:00:00Z"
    crawl_item = {
        "connection_id": "test-connection-id",
        "function_name": "get_bills",
        "submit": {
            "tasks_started": {"submit_task_id_1"},
            "tasks_finished": {"submit_task_id_1"},
            "set_latest_data": window_end,
        },
    }
    mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.get_scheduler_row", return_value=crawl_item)
    commit_mock = mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.commit_latest_data")

    crawler.wait_for_window_commit("test-connection-id", "get_bills", window_end)

    commit_mock.assert_called_once_with("test-connection-id", "get_bills", crawl_item)

    now_mock.side_effect = [

        start + timedelta(seconds=CRAWL_WINDOW_COMMIT_TIMEOUT + 1),

content.text:
Done. TRA-2689 filed for the bug: [Crawler tail overwrites latest_data_override with the full crawl end](https://linear.app/trackstar-hq/issue/TRA-2689/crawler-tail-overwrites-latest-data-override-with-the-full-crawl-end).

**What landed** (branch `early-crawl-end`, uncommitted):

An integration returns `crawl_window_end` alongside `data`, with `next_token` None. `resources/base_resource.py:620` enforces that (and that it isn't combined with `latest_data_override`); the crawler additionally rejects a window end outside `(window start, crawl end]`, so a bad value can't loop or skip.

The loop (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:438-510`) arms `set_latest_data = window_end`, waits for that window's submits to drain, then advances `start_time_dt` and resets the token, all inside the same `while`. `wait_for_window_commit` polls the scheduler row and writes the watermark itself if the last submitter finished before it was armed — without that it would deadlock on the race the tail block already handles.

`submit.is_final_commit` is the new flag distinguishing a window commit from the crawl ending. `handle_scheduler_crawl_items` returns it as `finished_last_page`, so the historical-sync and force-sync-completed webhooks fire once at the true end instead of on window 1. The tail checks it too, since `max_pages` can break out mid-window.

Both commit paths now go through one `commit_latest_data` in `lambda_handlers/submitter.py:180` (it had to live there, not in the crawler, or the import cycles). That incidentally fixes TRA-2689 — the tail reads `set_latest_data` off the row now instead of hardcoding `end_time_str`. Say the word if you'd rather I pull that out and ship it separately.

Sync jobs get windowing for free without committing anything: a finished window no longer sets `mark_complete`. FBA's `and not sync_job_id` guard becomes unnecessary.

`yarn test nonints`: 583 passed, 1 failed — `test_openapi`, which is a local env thing (`openapi2postmanv2` can't find `../dist/index.js` in this worktree's node_modules), unrelated. Six new tests cover window advance, the range guard, both `wait_for_window_commit` branches, and the two `finished_last_page` outcomes. I also made `update_crawl_items_mock` model dynamo properly (ALL_NEW returns the accumulated row, `tasks_started`/`tasks_finished` union rather than replace) — the old fixture returned only the write it just made, which is why the tail could never see an armed watermark in tests.

**On leveraging `current_crawl_start` more.** Yes, and I think the interesting version is decoupling the two jobs `latest_data` currently does at once. It's both "where do I resume" and "how caught up am I" — the second is what `stale_schedule_marker.py:446-464` and the customer-facing sync status read. Windowing is the first case where those want to move at different speeds.

If `current_crawl_start` is the authoritative resume pointer, the barrier stops being needed for correctness. You'd advance `current_crawl_start` per window immediately, keep crawling, and let `latest_data` lag behind at whatever the submitters have actually drained. A task that dies mid-window-5 resumes at window 5, the rows from windows 1-4 are already in dynamo, and `latest_data` self-corrects on the next completion. Throughput stops being coupled to lambda round-trips.

Two things to work out before that's real. `store_current_crawl_params` is opt-in and documented as only useful when `store_page_token` is on (`resources/base_resource.py:94`), so windowed mode would need to force it on rather than trusting each integration. And a task that dies leaves `latest_data` looking stale for real to the stale marker, so it needs to learn that a schedule whose `current_crawl_start` is advancing is making progress even when the watermark isn't. That second one is worth doing on its own merits — it's the same false-positive that any long first crawl produces today.

I'd ship the barrier version first and treat the decoupling as the follow-up once we've seen a windowed integration in prod. Want me to convert Finale get_orders onto this now, or file the `current_crawl_start` follow-up as its own card first?

Lets a crawl commit a watermark partway through its range and keep going, so an integration whose filter can't cover the whole window doesn't have to smuggle the leftover range through its page token.

Stacked on #5671. Base it there until that merges.

The case: a crawl asks for 45 days but the source API's filter only supports 30. Today the integration has to encode "resume at day 30" into its page token, which makes the token stateful, awkward to reason about mid-crawl, and a recurring source of stale-schedule hand-holding. Finale `get_orders` is the current example, chaining 4-hour windows through the token.

Now the integration returns `crawl_window_end` alongside its data, with `next_token` None. The crawler commits that watermark, advances the start, and continues in the same loop. Progress becomes durable at window granularity: a task that dies at window 5 of 270 resumes at window 5, with no token to go stale.

## What changed

- `crawl_window_end` on the crawl schema. `validate_crawl` rejects it alongside `next_token` or `latest_data_override`; the crawler rejects a value outside `(window start, crawl end]`, so a bad one can't loop or skip.
- The crawl loop arms `set_latest_data`, waits for that window's submit tasks to drain, then advances. `wait_for_window_commit` writes the watermark itself if the last submitter finished before it was armed. Without that it would wait forever on the same race the tail block already handles.
- `submit.is_final_commit` separates a window commit from the crawl ending. `handle_scheduler_crawl_items` returns it as `finished_last_page`, so the historical-sync and force-sync-completed webhooks fire once at the true end rather than on window 1. The tail checks it too, since `max_pages` can break out mid-window.
- `current_crawl_start` advances per window with `current_crawl_end` pinned, so a resumed crawl keeps the same end instead of letting it slide forward.
- Sync jobs get windowing without committing anything: a finished window no longer sets `mark_complete`. This is what FBA's `and not sync_job_id` guard exists to work around, so that can come out later.

Nothing calls this yet. Finale `get_orders` is the intended first caller, in a follow-up.

## Tradeoff worth knowing

A windowed crawl drains backlog at one window per scheduler tick, where page-token chaining drains it all inside one task. Finale's 4-hour window against orders' 1-hour frequency catches up at 4x, but an integration whose window is smaller than its crawl frequency would never converge, and `latest_data` is what the stale-schedule marker keys off. Worth a look at each caller's window size before converting it.

content.text:
Greptile's mechanism is wrong, but it's pointing at a real gap next to it.

The claim is that the fixture "fabricates an all-tasks-finished state." It doesn't. Greptile read the sentinel injection at `crawl_test.py:181-182` without accounting for the union merge right below it at 191-195. I replayed the actual call sequence (two pages, then the tail's `last_crawl_end` write):

```
submit after tail write: {'tasks_started': {'', 'submit_task_id_1', 'submit_task_id_2'},
                          'tasks_finished': {''},
                          'set_latest_data': '1999-06-01T00:00:00Z'}
should_update_latest_data: False
```

The sentinel unions into the sets rather than replacing them, so `tasks_started != tasks_finished` and completion is never fabricated. The regression test doesn't lean on it either — it patches `should_update_latest_data` to True explicitly, which is the honest way to pin the crawler-wins-the-race branch.

The injection itself is unrealistic, though: dynamo wouldn't touch `submit` on an update that omits it. It's there only because `test_first_crawl` asserts on the mutated call args, and it predates my change. Worth cleaning up, but it's cosmetic.

**The thing actually worth looking out for**, which Greptile is circling without naming: nothing in the suite drives the real drain transition. Every test that reaches the commit either forces `should_update_latest_data` to True or mocks the row. No test has the submitter mark tasks finished and watches `started == finished` flip naturally. That's a tolerable gap on #5671, where the commit is a one-shot at the end of a crawl.

It matters more on #5673. `wait_for_window_commit` polls for exactly that transition, and my tests there mock `get_scheduler_row` (the helper's unit tests) or mock the helper itself (the loop test). So the barrier's interaction with a genuinely draining row is untested, and that's the piece most likely to hang in prod. I'd add a test on that PR that steps a row from armed-and-undrained to drained across two polls and asserts the barrier returns rather than raising.

Want me to reply to the Greptile thread with the disproof, and add that barrier test to #5673?

Both done.

**Greptile reply** on #5671: https://github.com/trackstarhq/pokedex/pull/5671#discussion_r3844606655 — posted the replayed call sequence showing `should_update_latest_data` is `False` after the tail write, so no fabricated completion, and acknowledged the injection is unrealistic modeling that predates the PR. Left the thread unresolved since it's Greptile's to close.

**Barrier coverage** on #5673, commit `10d91dc94`: a row stepping from armed-and-undrained to drained across two polls (asserting the barrier returns and commits with the drained row), plus the case where the submitter already wrote the watermark and the barrier should return without committing.

Two things worth flagging from doing it:

The existing barrier tests could hang rather than fail. They polled one `return_value` row with a real `sleep`, and `now()` is frozen by the autouse fixture, so a barrier that stopped committing would spin forever instead of failing — I hit exactly that while mutation-testing. Finite `side_effect` rows and a mocked `sleep` now make a regression fail in seconds. Worth knowing generally: any test touching `wait_for_window_commit` needs `sleep` mocked, because the frozen clock defeats the timeout that bounds it in production.

I verified the new tests aren't vacuous by stubbing the commit branch to `if False:` — both fail with `StopIteration` as intended, and the file is restored (`git diff` on `celery_tasks/crawler.py` is empty). `yarn test celery lambda`: 198 passed. PR body updated from six tests to eight.

10	
11	- **Integration PR** (touches `integrations/{type}/{name}/` and/or its `test/integrations/{type}/{name}_test.py`): set `test override: ` `yarn test -k <name>` — the integration name only, no scope arg before `-k`. A stale-schedule or single-integration fix is always one integration; a change that reaches the framework is a non-integration PR (below).
12	- **Multi-integration sweep PR** (a `/fix-tests` run touching several integrations, nothing outside them): repeat the flag per integration — `test override: ` `yarn test -k <a> -k <b> -k <c>` — listing exactly the integrations whose files changed. Same arg shape CI auto-detect emits; `scripts/test.py` resolves each `-k` to its test file.
13	- **Non-integration PR** (anything else — `utils/`, `resources/`, `celery_tasks/`, `config.py`, `lambda_handlers/`, `api.py`, `scripts/`, etc.): set `test override: ` `yarn test nonints`. Run the non-integration suite — do **not** let the full integration suite run (it is slow and hits real/sandbox vendor APIs).
14	- **No test-affecting change** (docs / markdown / config only): put `[skip-tests]` in the body.
15	
16	**Why:** leave the default `-s` and CI auto-detects from the diff, falling back to the **full integration suite** the moment a non-integration file appears — slow, flaky, and vendor-hitting. An explicit `-k <name>` (integration) or `nonints` (everything else) keeps CI fast and deterministic.
17	
18	## Ship on merge
19	
20	The template's ship block (between the `<!-- ship-on-merge -->` markers) is a deploy request. Merging a PR whose body has a stage and at least one service ticked dispatches `ship.yml` for exactly those services, then comments on the PR naming the run, who merged it, and who last edited the body.
21	
22	- **Untouched ships nothing**, and so does a body with no ship block at all, which is what every PR built from a skill template has. Leave those templates alone: a PR opened unattended must not be able to deploy.
23	- **Tick it yourself, when you mean it.** Anyone with write access can edit a body after approval and after merge, so the boxes carry no review gate. Prod is a real release; it is recorded, not gated.
24	- **`crawler` is not a free tick.** The rollout stops the running tasks. A crawl in flight is killed rather than retried, only recovers once its heartbeat goes stale up to 10 minutes later, and for almost every integration then restarts from page 1.
25	- **The names are `config.SERVICES` keys.** An unknown or misspelled one fails the merge run loudly instead of quietly shipping a subset. `test/utils/ship_on_merge_test.py` keeps the boxes and config in step.
26	
27	## Investigation and fix PRs
28	
29	- **The diff must contain the fix the body claims.** A PR describing a code fix with an empty or unrelated diff gets closed on sight. Before opening, verify the branch actually carries the change — and that the same fix hasn't already landed on `main` through another PR.
30	- **Include the raw data that proves the diagnosis** — the source API rows, log lines, or Datadog query behind the root-cause claim (redacted of customer PII) — in the PR body or a comment, so a human can verify the finding without re-running the investigation.
31	
32	## Draft vs open

content.text:
Rebased onto `main` (which now has #5671 as `7b897a857`), no conflicts, force-pushed. PR #5673 auto-retargeted to `main` and is down to its own two commits: 354 insertions across 6 files. `yarn test nonints`: 610 passed, 2 failures that are both this worktree's environment (`test_openapi` can't resolve `openapi2postmanv2`'s dist, `test_integration_info_filters` hung on an SSL read). Neither touches crawler or submitter code, and `yarn test celery lambda` is 198/198.

## What the PR does

An integration whose filter can't cover the whole requested range returns `crawl_window_end` alongside its data, with `next_token` None. The crawler commits that watermark, advances the start, and keeps going in the same loop. The leftover range stops needing to live inside the page token.

Mechanically, three pieces. `crawl_window_end` on the crawl schema, with `validate_crawl` rejecting it next to `next_token` or `latest_data_override`, and the crawler rejecting a value outside `(window start, crawl end]`. A barrier, `wait_for_window_commit`, that arms `set_latest_data` and waits for that window's submits to drain before advancing, writing the watermark itself if the last submitter finished before it was armed. And `submit.is_final_commit`, which keeps the historical-sync and force-sync-completed webhooks firing once at the true end rather than on window 1.

The payoff is that progress becomes durable at window granularity: a task that dies at window 5 of 270 resumes at window 5, with no page token to go stale.

## What to think about

**Rollout ordering is the one real hazard, and right now you're safe from it.** `is_final_commit` is written by the crawler and read by the submitter lambda. A crawler that arms `is_final_commit: False` against an older submitter would get a premature historical-sync webhook, since the old submitter returns `should_update_latest_data` directly. Nothing sets `crawl_window_end` today (I checked `integrations/`), so the flag is always `True` and this PR is inert on its own. That's what makes it shippable independently. The rule it creates: the Finale conversion must not ship until both crawler and submitter are carrying this.

Also note `.claude/rules/pull-requests.md` grew a ship-on-merge section since we started, and it calls out that ticking `crawler` stops the running tasks: in-flight crawls are killed, recover only when the heartbeat goes stale up to 10 minutes later, and most integrations restart from page 1. Worth deciding deliberately when you merge this.

**Drain rate per caller.** A windowed crawl advances one window per scheduler tick, where token chaining drains the whole backlog inside one task. Finale's 4-hour window against orders' 1-hour frequency catches up at 4x, fine. An integration whose window is smaller than its crawl frequency never converges, and `latest_data` is exactly what `stale_schedule_marker.py` keys off, so it would go stale and stay stale. Right now that check is eyeballing. It might be worth making the window size a declared property on the resource so the framework can compute the ratio and refuse or warn, rather than trusting each integration author to do the arithmetic.

**The barrier is the part I'd expect to want gone.** It costs a lambda round-trip per window and is the piece most likely to misbehave in prod. The follow-up we discussed removes it: make `current_crawl_start` the authoritative resume pointer, advance it per window without waiting, and let `latest_data` lag at whatever has actually drained. That needs `store_current_crawl_params` forced on for windowed mode, and needs the stale marker to understand that an advancing `current_crawl_start` means progress even when the watermark is frozen. That second half is worth doing regardless, since it's the same false positive any long first crawl produces today.

**Smaller cleanups this unblocks.** FBA's `and not sync_job_id` guard in `get_inventory_ledger` exists to work around sync jobs having no watermark; sync jobs now window without committing anything, so it can come out. And Finale `get_orders` is the natural first caller, converting `integration.py:528-577` from token chaining to a `crawl_window_end` return.

My suggestion for sequencing: mark #5673 ready and get a human read on the barrier semantics, merge it inert, then do Finale as a separate PR where you can watch one real connection's drain rate before deciding whether the decoupling follow-up is worth building.

content.text:
Here's the matrix as it behaves today. Both axes are what the integration returns from one page; `data` is orthogonal (any cell can carry rows or be empty).

| | **`crawl_window_end` is None** | **`crawl_window_end` = W** |
|---|---|---|
| **`next_token` is None** | **Crawl over.** Arms `set_latest_data = end_time_str`, `is_final_commit=True`. Clears `current_crawl_start`/`current_crawl_end`, drops the page token, exits the loop. The submitter (or the tail, whoever wins) writes `latest_data` and fires the historical-sync / force-sync webhooks. | **Window boundary.** Arms `set_latest_data = W`, `is_final_commit=False`. Writes `current_crawl_start = W` with `current_crawl_end` pinned, clears the page token, waits for the barrier, advances `start_time_dt` to W, resets the token to `"default"`, loops. No webhooks. |
| **`next_token` = X** | **More pages in the same window.** Stores X as `latest_page_token`, keeps `current_crawl_start` where it is, loops with the same start. No watermark armed, so nothing commits. | **Invalid.** `validate_crawl` (`resources/base_resource.py:622-626`) rejects it. A window can't be finished while pages remain inside it, and honoring both would mean committing a watermark over data not yet fetched. |

The cell you're asking about, "window done and that was also the last one," isn't missing. It's already a separate key: `latest_data_override` means commit this watermark and stop, which is exactly FBA's short final window. `crawl_window_end` means commit this watermark and continue. They're mutually exclusive by validation, and together they cover both endings.

So no, I don't think a new key is needed. But two things fall out of laying it out this way, and both are real.

**`window_end == end_time_str` costs a wasted round trip.** The guard allows `window_start < W <= end`, so an integration whose window lands exactly on the crawl end commits W, advances, and then calls the integration again with `start == end` — a zero-width query whose only job is to come back empty so the crawl can conclude at cell 1. Correct, but a wasted vendor call per crawl, and a weird edge for the integration to handle. Tightening the guard to `<` is the wrong fix (a legal boundary would blow up the crawl). The right fix is one condition in the crawler: if `W == end_time_str`, treat it as the final commit and exit instead of looping. Finale's natural shape (`if filter_end < end`) never hits this, but an integration that computes windows slightly differently would.

**`crawl_window_end` + `pending_page_token` is an unvalidated contradiction.** Royal Mail's `pending_page_token` means "store this state and exit gracefully, don't commit a watermark." If an integration returned both, `crawler.py:466-470` arms the watermark *and* writes `latest_page_token = pending_page_token`, then the loop advances past it with `next_token = "default"` and the pending token is stranded on the row for a crawl that no longer wants it. Nothing catches this today. It belongs in the same `validate_crawl` block as the other two assertions.

If it's worth making the whole decision point legible rather than three keys an author has to know about, the alternative shape is one key with an explicit continuation: something like `crawl_window = {"end": W, "more": True|False}`, where `more: False` subsumes `latest_data_override`. That's a bigger refactor touching FBA and Royal Mail, and I'd only do it if we expect more than a couple of windowed integrations. For two or three callers, three well-validated keys is fine.

Want me to add the `W == end` short-circuit and the missing validation to #5673?

content.text:
Your instinct about the top-right cell is right, but the specific failure you're picturing is already caught, and the one that isn't wouldn't go stale.

**Staleness is `latest_data` only.** `stale_schedule_marker.py:479`: `stale = now() - latest_data_dt > stale_threshold`, threshold being crawl frequency × multiplier. The page token doesn't enter into it, with exactly one exception, a hardcoded shiphero branch at 466-480 that substitutes the token because shiphero stuffs a timestamp in it. That branch is the hack windowing exists to replace.

Stuckness is a separate flag (`check_schedule_stuckness`, line 271) and *does* key off the token: `last_page_token_update or last_crawl_end or created_at`, stuck after 12h without movement.

So a runaway windowing loop is invisible to both. Every window commits `latest_data`, and every page writes `last_page_token_update`. It would look like the healthiest schedule in the fleet while one celery task spins forever. And there's no outer bound to catch it: `crawl_task` has no `soft_time_limit`, and `reject_on_worker_lost=True` means even getting killed by a deploy just re-queues it to resume from `current_crawl_start`.

**But the bug you described fails loudly already.** The guard is `window_start < W <= end_time_dt` (`crawler.py:443`). An integration that computes `W = start + 4h` and never checks against `end` raises `PokedexException` the moment a window would overshoot, on the first crawl that reaches the end of its range. Forgetting the terminating condition entirely is a fast, noisy failure, not a silent spin.

To actually escape the guard you'd need windows that approach `end` without reaching it. Two shapes:

- Zeno: `W = start + (end - start) / 2`. Always valid, never terminates. Contrived, but it's what "forgot to terminate" has to look like to slip past.
- Absurdly small windows: a 1-second window over a 45-day first crawl is 3.9M iterations, each with a barrier round trip. Not infinite, but effectively so, and it looks healthy the entire time.

The second one is the realistic risk. It isn't a forgotten `None`, it's a window size that's fine for a 4-hour incremental crawl and catastrophic for the 30-day first crawl.

**What I'd add**, and yes it's testable:

A window cap per task, the same shape as `max_pages` but not opt-in: count committed windows, raise a `PokedexException` past some ceiling. That bounds both shapes with one condition and turns an invisible spin into a normal crawl error, which is the failure mode we already have alerting for. The test is cheap and direct: an integration that always returns `crawl_window_end` halving the remaining range, asserting the crawler raises after N windows instead of looping. That's the validation you're asking for, and it exercises the top-right cell staying occupied forever.

Longer term, the stronger version is having the resource declare its window size, so the crawler can multiply it against the first-crawl lookback and refuse a configuration that implies 3.9M windows *before* making a single vendor call, rather than discovering it 500 windows in. That's the same declaration that would let us automate the drain-rate check I flagged earlier, so the two land together.

Want me to add the cap plus that test to #5673, and pick a ceiling? I'd start somewhere around 500, which covers Finale's 30-day first crawl at 4-hour windows (180) with room, and is nowhere near the pathological cases.

content.text:
Fair. "Commit" is transaction/git vocabulary borrowed for something that's neither: nothing is atomic, nothing rolls back. It's just a forward-only pointer being written to a dynamo row, and the repo's own one-read test says don't make a reader translate.

What I'd use instead, drawing on words already in this code:

- `commit_latest_data` → **`advance_latest_data`**. The watermark only ever moves forward, so "advance" says the actual constraint. Prose becomes "the watermark advances" rather than "we commit a watermark."
- `wait_for_window_commit` → **`wait_for_submit_drain`**. This one's already sitting there: the function's own log line says "Waiting for submit tasks to drain," and `clean_up_crawl_submit` is in the same family. Name it what it waits for.
- `submit.is_final_commit` → **`submit.mark_complete`**.

That last one is the interesting one. The sync-job path already has `submit.mark_complete` (`crawler.py:461`, read by `should_sync_job_complete` at `utils/boto.py:2906`) meaning exactly this: last page, so finish the thing when the submits drain. My flag invented a second word for an idea the codebase already names. Reusing it means the crawl path and the sync path express "this is the end" identically instead of two ways, and the backward-compat read is the same shape (`.get("mark_complete", True)`).

The one argument against is that a reader might expect crawl `mark_complete` to trigger sync-job logic. They're different rows and different readers, so I think the symmetry wins, but `crawl_complete` is the fallback if you'd rather keep them visibly distinct.

For prose I'd drop "commit" entirely: **window boundary** for the event, **the watermark advances** for the effect, **the window drains** for the wait.

Cost is 30 references across 4 files. Worth noting `commit_latest_data` merged in #5671, so renaming it touches code that's already on main — but #5673 edits those exact lines anyway, so this is the cheapest moment to do it, before anything else accretes around the name.

Want me to apply that rename to #5673, and does `mark_complete` or `crawl_complete` sit better with you?

    # a window's rows have to be stored before the crawl moves past it, otherwise a
    # task that dies in the next window would resume after data that never landed
    logger.info(f"Waiting for submit tasks to drain through {window_end}")
    deadline = now() + timedelta(seconds=CRAWL_WINDOW_DRAIN_TIMEOUT)
    while now() < deadline:

content.text:
No code changed. Here are the options, with what each gets right and wrong.

**`next_start`** (my recommendation). It pairs with `next_token` as the two continuation signals, and the pairing *is* the semantics: `next_token` means more pages in the same range, `next_start` means this range is done, move forward. They're already mutually exclusive by validation, so the parallel naming makes the 2x2 chart read itself. The assertion becomes "next_token must be None when next_start is set," which needs no explanation. It also fixes a collision I think is part of what's bugging you: `get_orders(self, start, end, ...)` already has `end` as a parameter, so `crawl_window_end` sits three feet from a different `end` and is easy to misread. `next_start` sits next to `start` and means the next one.

**`complete_through`** (runner-up). States the safety-critical claim outright: everything from `start` to here has been fetched, so it can never be revisited. That's the thing an integration author must actually believe before setting it. `next_start` describes the mechanism and leaves the claim implicit, which is the one real strike against it: someone could read "where to resume" without registering "and I'm asserting the earlier range is fully done." If you want the name to do that teaching, this is the one. Costs the symmetry with `next_token`.

**`resume_from`**. Clear, no collision, obviously a continuation. But it's `next_start` with a worse pairing and the same implicitness problem, so I'd only take it if "start" feels overloaded to you.

**`set_latest_data`** — I'd avoid this one. It's already a field name on the scheduler row (`submit.set_latest_data`), and the row field is the general sink, fed from three sources: this key, `latest_data_override`, and the plain `end_time_str`. Naming one source identically to the sink makes them look like the same thing. It also points the integration author at scheduler-row internals they otherwise never need to know about, which is backwards for a key that's part of the integration-facing contract.

If you pick `next_start`, the rename reaches a bit further than the key: the loop variable `window_end`, the `wait_for_submit_drain` parameter, the two `CRAWL_WINDOW_DRAIN_*` constants (probably `SUBMIT_DRAIN_*`), and the test names. Still small, and cheaper now than after a caller exists.

One thing worth deciding alongside it: "window" survives in the constants, the comments, and how we talk about this. If `next_start` wins, we could drop the window vocabulary entirely and describe it as the crawl advancing its start, which is one less concept. Or keep "window" as the informal word for the chunk while the key itself says `next_start`. I lean toward dropping it.

content.text:
Renamed and pushed (`96a4e65c0`), on top of your "shrink some comments" commit. `yarn test celery lambda`: 198 passed. I kept "window" in comments and test names, dropped it from the key, and made the constants `SUBMIT_DRAIN_TIMEOUT` / `_POLL` (they bound the submitter, not the chunk) with `window_start_str` → `current_start_str`, which is what it feeds.

**On the window vocabulary, I overstated it.** `next_start` doesn't remove the concept, it removes it from the *contract*. An integration author returning `next_start` never has to learn what a window is; they say "call me again from here." But the chunk between `start` and `next_start` is still a real thing the framework needs a word for: it's what `wait_for_submit_drain` waits on, what a cap would count, what the comments describe. "Window" is the right word for that and I left it there.

**On staleness, you're right and I was wrong.** A runaway *does* go stale, and the reason is `end`. It's pinned at crawl start and the guard caps `next_start` at it, so `latest_data` can never advance past the moment the crawl began. Real time keeps moving, `now() - latest_data` grows without bound, and it crosses the threshold. That's true for the tiny-window case and for the halving case I claimed was invisible.

Threshold is `crawl_frequency × STALE_CRAWL_MULTIPLIER` (`config.py:1000`, which is 12; carriers use 2). Orders at 1h means flagged 12h in. Stuck won't fire, since `check_schedule_stuckness` keys off `last_page_token_update` and every page writes it, but stale is enough.

**Except on a first crawl, where windowing opens a hole that didn't exist before.** Tracing it properly:

- `is_first_crawl_unfinished = last_crawl_start and not latest_data` (`stale_schedule_marker.py:398`). Once the first window advances `latest_data`, the row stops qualifying and falls through.
- The regular path then hits `if not latest_data or not last_crawl_end: continue` (`:438`). A first crawl still running has never written `last_crawl_end`, so the row is skipped entirely.

So a runaway first crawl is invisible to both branches until the task dies and writes `last_crawl_end`. And this is specifically created by windowing: before it, `latest_data` was never set mid-crawl, so "latest_data present, last_crawl_end absent" wasn't a reachable state. A 30-day first crawl is also exactly where a bad window size does the most damage.

The fix is small and belongs in this PR since this PR creates the state: key the first-crawl branch on `last_crawl_start and not last_crawl_end` (started, never finished) rather than on `latest_data` being absent. That keeps a windowed first crawl under first-crawl staleness detection where it belongs.

The cap still earns its place, but for a narrower reason than I gave: not "the only way we'd find out," but "fail in one crawl instead of burning a worker for 12 hours." A spinning task also blocks the connection from crawling at all, since `crawl_heartbeat_active` prevents re-enqueue, so that window is 12 hours of no data rather than just delayed alerting.

Want me to take the stale-marker fix, the cap plus halving test, and the `next_start == end` short-circuit as one more commit on this branch?

That's the invariant windowing breaks, and it's worse than the stale-marker hole I flagged. That hole is just one symptom.

`first_crawl` is derived in the scheduler as "no `latest_data` yet" (`scheduler.py:104-105`), which is exactly how it survives failures the way you describe: a first crawl that dies writes `last_crawl_end`, but `latest_data` stays unset, so the next attempt is still a first crawl. `latest_data` is doing double duty as both "how far we've gotten" and "the historical backfill is done." Windowing sets it at the first window boundary, which separates those two meanings for the first time and silently declares the backfill finished after one window.

Four things break, in rough order of how bad:

**Per-row webhooks start firing mid-backfill.** `submitter.py:133`: `if first_crawl: return` is what keeps a backfill from webhooking every row. Once the flag flips, the remaining ~29 days of a 30-day lookback fire `.created`/`.updated` at the customer, one per row.

**The historical-sync-completed webhook never fires.** `submitter.py:108` gates on `first_crawl and finished_last_page`, and by the time the backfill actually reaches its end, `first_crawl` is False. So `set_connections_historical_sync_completed` never runs and the customer never gets told the backfill finished.

**Dependent resources unblock early.** `check_first_crawl_complete` returns True the moment `latest_data` exists (`base_resource.py:930`). Finale's `get_orders` calls `Product(self).check_first_crawl_complete()` before reading the stored product catalog for kit expansion, so it would unblock after one window of products and expand kits against a partial catalog. That's the intended first caller, hitting this on its own dependency.

**Stale detection loses the row**, as I described: it stops qualifying as a first crawl and, without `last_crawl_end` on the very first attempt, gets skipped by the regular branch too.

The fix is to stop inferring "backfill complete" from `latest_data`. I'd add an explicit scheduler-row flag, set when a crawl reaches its true end (the same `mark_complete` moment that already distinguishes the end from a window boundary), with the scheduler reading `first_crawl = not first_crawl_complete` and `check_first_crawl_complete` reading the same flag. Existing rows have `latest_data` and no flag, so those get treated as complete and nothing on the fleet changes.

The cheap alternative is to refuse `next_start` when `first_crawl` is True, so windowing only applies to incremental crawls. That's a one-line guard and it's safe, but it gives up the case windowing helps most, since the 30-day backfill is where the leftover range actually hurts.

I'd do the flag. It's a small change but it touches the scheduler and the first-crawl contract, so worth you agreeing on the shape before I write it. Want me to take that, plus the stale-marker branch, the window cap, and the `next_start == end` short-circuit, as one commit or split up?

content.text:
Generally yes, and it's a nice instinct because it needs no new field and existing rows answer it correctly on their own. The historical range is `created_at - lookback` → `end`, so `latest_data` passing `created_at` does mean the historical part is covered.

Two things to square first, one of which bites either approach.

**The bigger one, independent of the rule.** `crawler.py:253-269` overwrites `start_time_str` with `created_at - lookback` unconditionally whenever `first_crawl` is True. Today that's harmless, because a first crawl that dies has no progress to lose and genuinely should restart from June 1. With windowing it's destructive: your rule keeps `first_crawl` True through the backfill, so a task that dies at June 20 comes back, gets reset to June 1, and re-crawls everything it already did. If it keeps dying it never converges. That override has to become conditional on there being no progress yet, whichever way we define "first crawl done."

**The anchor is slightly off.** The range ends at `now()` when the crawl starts, not at `created_at`. When the first crawl runs promptly that gap is minutes and the rule is fine. Two cases where it isn't:

- *A delayed first crawl.* Connection created July 1, but bad credentials or a pause mean the first crawl doesn't run until July 10. Range is June 1 → July 10. `latest_data` crosses July 1 with nine days left, so we'd declare the backfill done and per-row webhook the rest.
- *A function enabled long after the connection.* The lookback still anchors on the connection's `created_at`, so a function turned on a year later gets a range of `created_at - 30d` → now, about thirteen months. Your rule calls it done after the first thirty days and the remaining year backfills with per-row webhooks firing at the customer. That one isn't exotic and the blast radius is large.

The exact form of what you're describing is "`latest_data` reached the first crawl's `end`," and `created_at` is a proxy for that end that's good when the crawl runs immediately. That exact moment is one we're already identifying, since it's the same `mark_complete` that separates the crawl ending from a window boundary.

So my read: your rule is right about *when*, and I'd write it down at that moment rather than re-derive it from `created_at` afterward. Persisting one boolean when the crawl reaches its end is the same amount of work as the comparison, can't drift as `end` and `created_at` diverge, and `check_first_crawl_complete` can read the same thing instead of its current `latest_data` check. Rows that already have `latest_data` and no flag read as complete, so nothing on the fleet moves.

If you'd rather avoid the field, the comparison works with a floor: treat the first crawl as done only when `latest_data >= max(created_at, first crawl's end)` — but that needs the end persisted, which is the field again by another name.

Either way I'd fix the `start_time_str` override in the same change, since it's load-bearing for resume.

content.text:
Two answers, and the second is better news than I gave you.

**Resume: the row saves it, the crawler throws it away.** The scheduler does pass `current_crawl_start` as the start (`scheduler.py:107-112`), but `crawler.py:253-269` overwrites it with `created_at - lookback` whenever `first_crawl` is True. It's harmless today only because a first crawl's `current_crawl_start` never moves — every page writes the same original start — so the overwrite recomputes the identical value. Windowing is what makes it move, which turns that no-op into throwing away real progress. So no, `current_crawl_params` doesn't save you on its own; it needs that override guarded on there being no progress yet. Same for the page token: it's stored on first crawls too, but at a window boundary `next_token` is None, so the token isn't the resume state anymore, `current_crawl_start` is.

**Anchor: yes, largely.** I undersold `store_current_crawl_params` earlier by calling it opt-in. It defaults to **True** at the `WMSIntegration` level for products, orders, inbound shipments, and bills (`WMSIntegration.py:60,125,163,285`), with only two integrations overriding it. So `current_crawl_end` is broadly available, and during a first crawl it holds that crawl's true end. `latest_data < current_crawl_end` is then an exact "still backfilling" test, with no `created_at` proxy and none of the delayed-start or enabled-a-year-later error.

The one thing it can't do alone is tell you *which* crawl it's describing. An interrupted incremental crawl populates the same two fields, so `latest_data < current_crawl_end` is also true for a normal multi-page crawl whose task died. Pairing it with your `created_at` rule covers the common case, since an incremental crawl always has `latest_data >= created_at`, and the pair only disagrees in exactly the year-later case.

If you want it unambiguous, there's already a flag for this and it isn't a new field: `historical_sync_completed[function_name]` on the connection row, written by `set_connections_historical_sync_completed`. It means precisely "the backfill for this function finished." Today it's written from `handle_historical_sync_webhooks`, which is gated on `first_crawl`, so it can't be the input to `first_crawl` as-is. Writing it at the `mark_complete` moment instead breaks that circle and makes `first_crawl = not historical_sync_completed.get(function_name)` exact. The wrinkle to check is backfilling it for existing connections, since `suppress_webhooks()` resources never set it, so the derivation would need to fall back to today's `not latest_data` where the flag is absent.

My read: guard the start override either way, then pick between your `created_at` rule (simplest, wrong only for a function enabled long after its connection) and reusing `historical_sync_completed` (exact, needs a backward-compat fallback). Which do you want?
